extracted.intended_audience: general readers; mathematicians; students interested in the history and status of important mathematical problems
extracted.subtask_description: A general encyclopedic overview of David Hilbert's list of 23 (originally 24) mathematical problems: statement headers, brief explanations, and current status/interpretive remarks. Useful as a reference for history, status, and influence of the problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of problem formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hilbert's problems ranged greatly in topic and precision. Some of them, like the 3rd problem ... or the 8th problem (the Riemann hypothesis), ... were presented precisely enough to enable a clear affirmative or negative answer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: a problem should be formulated with sufficient precision to permit a definite yes/no (or equally sharply decisive) resolution. Example/anti-pattern: problems stated only suggestively or vaguely are less likely to admit a single, accepted solution. The page emphasizes that precisely stated problems attracted clear solutions and major progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus-based resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of the cleanly formulated Hilbert problems: 3, 6a, 7, 10, 11, 14, 17, 18, 19, and 21 have resolutions that are accepted by consensus of the mathematical community."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: whether a problem is 'solved' often depends on community acceptance of the purported solution (proof correctness, agreement on interpretation). Use community consensus as an evaluative standard when declaring a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial or partial solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The status of problems 1, 2, 5, 6b, 8c, 13, and 15 is controversial: there are some results, but there exists some controversy as to whether they resolve the problems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: some published results may be incomplete, depend on particular formalizations, or be disputed; such results should be classified as 'controversial' rather than definitively solved. Provide explicit statements of assumptions/interpretations and note open points of contention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unresolved despite partial results
rubrics_metrics.description: "Problems 8a, 8b, 9, 12, 16, 20 and 22 are unresolved or widely agreed as unresolved despite some partial results."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: record partial advances and clarify which aspects remain open. Distinguish between partial progress (special cases, numerical evidence, conditional results) and a full resolution; do not conflate the two when reporting status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too vague to be described as solved
rubrics_metrics.description: "Problems 4 and 23 are considered as too vague to ever be described as solved; the withdrawn 24 would also be in this class."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: for problems lacking sufficient precision, the appropriate classification is 'too vague.' Such items may serve more as programmatic suggestions than precise conjectures; avoid declaring them solved without a clear, agreed formal restatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation-dependent solvability
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated notes like "Depends on the interpretation of the problem" (examples: Hilbert's 5th, 6th, 8c, 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: many of Hilbert's items admit multiple natural formalizations; the truth/solvability can change with interpretation. When evaluating progress, specify which interpretation is being addressed and justify why that interpretation is the accepted one (or state that the issue remains interpretation-dependent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness and specialness as selection principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert's remark: "I have generally mentioned problems as definite and special as possible, in the opinion that it is just such definite and special problems that attract us the most and from which the most lasting influence is often exerted upon science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: for choosing or formulating influential problems, prefer definite, specific questions rather than vague programmatic statements. The historical lesson: specificity tends to attract concerted effort and lasting impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem inclusion to highlight an area (general indication)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The 23rd problem was purposefully set as a general indication by Hilbert to highlight the calculus of variations ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: not every item on a problems list must be a tightly stated conjecture; some can be deliberate calls to develop or draw attention to a subject area. Such items should be classified and interpreted differently from precise conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-simplicity and methods criterion (Hilbert's unpublished 24th)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The '24th problem' (in proof theory, on a criterion for simplicity and general methods) ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: an explicit desideratum for evaluating mathematical proofs is simplicity (a criterion Hilbert considered). This invites development of objective or comparative measures of simplicity and general methods, and suggests that proof quality can be evaluated beyond mere correctness (e.g., elegance, economy, generality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Status-classification rubric used in the article
rubrics_metrics.description: The article's tabular/status scheme: entries are marked with statuses like Resolved (with year and result), Unresolved, Depends (on interpretation), Controversial, Too vague, Withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: when cataloging problems, use a structured status taxonomy (and provide justification and references): state the status, give the decisive results or key partial results, list year(s), and explain interpretive caveats. This helps readers understand both the mathematical and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence/importance as an evaluative measure
rubrics_metrics.description: "They were all unsolved at the time, and several proved to be very influential for 20th-century mathematics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: beyond solvability, a problem's importance can be judged by the subsequent mathematical development it spurred (new fields, methods, awards). When assessing a problem's significance, document major consequences (e.g., creation of subdisciplines, landmark theorems, prizes like Fields Medal) rather than only final resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's knowability principle ('no ignorabimus')
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert's conviction: "in mathematics there is not any 'ignorabimus' (statement whose truth can never be known)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: historically, Hilbert assumed that every mathematical problem should have a knowable solution (possibly a proof of impossibility). This philosophical stance influenced problem selection and evaluation; when discussing foundational problems, note how philosophical commitments about knowability and formalization affect claims of resolution.
